# A Dictionary of Kept Things

My grandmother left behind eleven notebooks, and in all of them, tucked between grocery lists and phone numbers and the tallies of card games, was the same quiet project: lists of words from her mother tongue, each one defined underneath in her careful, schoolroom English.

She never taught us the language. This was deliberate. When my father was a boy, she decided he would grow up sounding like everyone else — unmarked, unpointed-at in any classroom. So the language went underground, and these notebooks are what it did down there. For fifty years, while her English stayed plain and practical on the surface, she was below, tending a garden.

The earliest notebook begins the month she arrived, the ink faded to the color of weak tea. The last one ends two years ago. In between: thousands of words, each given its part of speech, its definition, and — this is the part I couldn't stop reading — an example sentence. Nobody writes themselves example sentences for half a century unless the examples are the point.

*Selvane*, she wrote. *The smell of rain arriving before the rain does. Hope announcing itself so that you cannot pretend you didn't hear.*

*Harnet. Work done before dawn for people who will never know it happened. Example: A woman rises at four o'clock. She irons the shirts of lawyers and doctors. When they admire the collars she says nothing, because the true word for what she did does not exist in this country, and anyway they are still asleep.*

My grandmother cleaned houses for thirty-one years. I knew that. What I didn't know was that she had been taking notes.

*Dovessa. Missing not a place but the person you were in that place. Example: The river is still there. I looked it up. But the girl who washed her hair in it is gone, and she is the one I miss.*

*Kirem. A kindness too large ever to repay, which can only be passed forward, like water handed along a line of thirsty strangers. Example: A man pays for a boy's ticket across an ocean and refuses his name. Sixty years later, the boy still sets an extra plate at every table.*

There is an extra plate at my mother's table. There always has been. None of us ever asked why.

*Ostavel. The silence a room keeps in the shape of whoever used to fill it. Example: Your grandfather's chair does not creak anymore. That is the silence I mean. It fits him exactly.*

*Lirren. To grieve and to give thanks in the same breath; to bury someone with one hand while setting their photograph facing the dinner table with the other. Example: Every morning I am angry at God and grateful to Him, often within the same cup of coffee.*

*Bruen. The held breath before speaking, when every sentence you might say still exists at once, whole and possible. Example: I stood on the dock with this word in my mouth. In some sense I have been standing there since.*

At first I read the notebooks as a hobby, the way some people do crosswords. Then somewhere in the fifth book I understood what I was holding. She was not translating. She was confessing in code. Memoirs disguised as lexicography. Every definition was a window she'd cut into the wall of the plain, practical English she showed us, and through each one I could see a room I had been living next to my entire life without knowing it was there.

Because here is the thing: she never used these words aloud. Not once. My father confirmed it, stunned, turning pages with hands that suddenly looked like hers. The language she gave up for our sake, she refused to let go of entirely — she just stopped speaking it and started keeping it instead. Some words are not for saying, she seemed to believe. They are for keeping, the way you keep seeds through winter: not because you doubt the spring, but because you want proof you expected it.

The final notebook is thin, its spine cracked. The last entry is dated three months before she died. It is a single line, in English, in handwriting larger than anything else in all eleven books, as if she wanted to be sure whoever found it would not miss it:

*If you are reading these, you are the example now.*

I sat with that for a long time. I'm sitting with it still. Because she was right, in the way she was right about everything, quietly and after the fact: the words don't end with her. A definition is a door, and she left every one of them open. *Kirem* — the kindness passed forward. *Selvane* — the hope that arrives ahead of itself. *Harnet* — the work done before dawn for people who will never know. I know that work now. I woke up this morning and made coffee in a silent kitchen and felt a silence that fit her exactly, and there is no English word for any of it, and for the first time in my life, that felt less like a loss than like an inheritance.

So tonight I bought a twelfth notebook. On the first page I copied her format exactly, the part of speech, the definition, the example. I don't have the word itself yet — she would have had it, filed somewhere between the grocery lists, patient as seed — but I have everything around it:

*_______. The thing you feel reading a dead woman's private dictionary and discovering that every definition, every example, all of them, was quietly, patiently, waiting for you. Example: A granddaughter opens a notebook. She reads until midnight. In the morning, she buys a pen.*

It isn't finished. Neither, it turns out, was she.

Neither, I think, are we supposed to be.

The user is giving me complete creative freedom — 1000 words, write whatever comes to me. This is an invitation for genuine creative expression. Let me think about what would be interesting to write.

I could do:
- A short story
- An essay/reflection
- A poem sequence
- A piece of experimental writing
- Something meta about the nature of the prompt itself

What feels most alive? The prompt "write whatever comes to you" is itself interesting — it's a blank canvas. I think a piece of creative prose that has some emotional depth and formal interest would be best. Let me try something that plays with the idea of... hmm.

Ideas:
1. A story about a lighthouse keeper who catalogs sounds
2. A meditation on memory told through objects in a junk drawer
3. A story from the perspective of something unusual (a word, a color, a house)
4. A piece about translation/loss of meaning
5. Something about time — maybe a person who receives letters from their future self
6. A vignette cycle about small moments

Let me go with something evocative. Maybe a story about someone whose job it is to listen — or perhaps something about a translator who realizes certain words don't survive the crossing between languages, and what that means about what we can actually say to each other. That's rich territory.

Or: a story about the last speaker of a language, and what dies with words. That's been done but can be done freshly.

Alternative: something quieter and stranger — a piece written as field notes from someone studying something mundane with absurd seriousness. Like "Notes on the Migration Patterns of Lost Socks" — humor plus poignancy.

Or: a letter format. A letter from a house to its inhabitants over centuries.

Let me try the translator idea, but make it concrete and human rather than abstract. A translator working on a dying woman's letters? Or — here's a thought — a person who translates for their immigrant grandmother, and after she dies, finds her notebooks full of words she never used, words she'd been collecting like pressed flowers. Words that had no English equivalent. And the narrator tries to build sentences out of them, tries to reconstruct the grandmother's inner life from the vocabulary she hoarded. That's emotionally resonant and formally interesting because I can invent words/concepts and describe them.

Structure:
1. Opening: finding the notebooks
2. The nature of the notebooks — lists of words from her language, each with definitions she wrote in careful English, but the definitions are really small essays
3. Some specific words (I'll invent them or borrow loosely) — each one revealing something about her life
4. Realization: these were words she never got to use; she was saving them
5. The narrator's attempt to speak/write using them, ending with something poignant

Word count target ~1000. Let me draft.

Words I might invent (or adapt): I should be careful not to claim they're real words from a real language — I'll keep the language unnamed, which also protects against misrepresenting an actual culture. Unnamed language, unnamed country. That's fine and even adds universality, though specificity usually strengthens fiction... I'll keep it lightly specified ("the old country," her village by the river) without naming a specific real language so I don't misuse real linguistic material.

Invented words:
- A word for "the light through leaves" — too cliché (komorebi exists). Instead:
- A word for grief that is also gratitude — mourning someone while thanking them
- A word for the smell of rain on flour/dough — kitchen memories
- A word for the distance between what you mean and what you say
- A word for homesickness that specifically means missing a place that no longer exists
- A word for the moment before speaking when everything is still possible
- A word for a debt of kindness that you can never repay, only pass forward
- A word for listening to someone sleep to be sure they're breathing
- A word for the particular silence of a room where someone has just died / or where someone used to live
- A word meaning "to carry water at dawn" extended to mean doing love's invisible work

Let me pick 4-6 strong ones and give each a little entry-style treatment, then frame narrative around it.

- Understanding the pattern: she collected words the way some people collect seeds

**A Dictionary of Kept Things**

My grandmother left behind eleven notebooks, and in all of them, hidden among grocery lists and addresses and the scores of card games, was the same quiet project: lists of words from her mother tongue, each one defined beneath in her careful schoolroom English.

She never taught us the language. This was deliberate. When my father was a boy, she decided he would grow up sounding like everyone else, unmarked, unhurried into any classroom as a foreigner. So the language went underground, and these notebooks are what it did down there. For fifty years, while her English stayed plain and practical on the surface, she was below, keeping a garden.
